prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect, and for its experimental discovery in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep B018 as my preferred configuration; this is not a change from round 1, but the exchange has sharpened why. The scientific core is a prediction with an identifiable origin (Kane and Mele: the Z2 invariant, Kramers-protected helical edge states, and the quantum spin Hall proposal) and a decisive measurement in a defined system (Molenkamp's HgTe/CdTe quantum wells, where edge-channel conductance showed the predicted quantised transport). The experiment is not a mere confirmation; it was the first realisation of a new symmetry-protected phase, and two decades of independent work in other materials and by other probes have left the interpretation stable. I am answering the chair's own question about the 2016 prize as follows: that prize recognised topological phase transitions and integer quantum Hall-type phases, whereas the time-reversal-invariant Z2 class with helical edges needs no magnetic field and is a distinct symmetry class with its own prediction and its own experiment. I therefore treat it as a separate discovery, not an overlap. I would write the citation narrowly around the quantum spin Hall state and say in deliberation that the 3D topological-insulator programme is not what is being recognised.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the real weakness and I do not think the committee should minimise it. The HgTe quantum-well proposal that guided Molenkamp's experiment came from Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, not from Kane and Mele; Zhang is deceased; and Bernevig and Hughes are outside the three-person set. A narrow citation reduces the problem but does not remove it, because the experiment followed a proposal that the credited theorists did not make. The 3D work (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Hasan and others) also sits at the boundary of the citation, and the 2016 prize may still weigh on some members' sense of whether this area has had its share. If the committee concludes that an acknowledged gap in the credit is disqualifying, B041 is the cleaner two-name case, and I would support it without reluctance.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock (B041) first, calls the Katori and Ye credit clean, and argues that the lattice with a magic wavelength is a distinct step from the 2005 comb and 2012 individual-quantum-system prizes.
responses.response: I accept your distinction from 2005 and 2012: neutral-atom ensembles with a lattice that cancels the clock-transition light shift are a different thing from combs or single trapped ions, and a citation anchored on the magic-wavelength lattice can be written plainly. That answers the chair's question about wording. Where I still differ is the criterion. The strength of B041 is attribution and reproducibility; its weakness, which you and Lindroth both name, is that it is an instrument and a measurement regime, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. Both clocks and topological insulators are mature, so I do not think maturity separates them. I weigh the new phase of matter above a new accuracy regime, and I weigh the attribution gap as a cost against B018 rather than as a veto. If we judge it a veto, I would vote for B041, and I expect you could say the same in reverse.

responses.point: Johansson prefers B041 but says that if a convincing lattice-clock citation cannot be written, B018 is the safer choice, and she lists B018 as her first alternative.
responses.response: This is the most useful statement in round 1 for settling the split, because it shows that the committee is not divided on quality. The two camps share the same two candidates and differ only on which defect they tolerate: B018 an incomplete credit, B041 an adjacent-precedent and evolutionary-step question. I think your conditional is the right form of the test. My own reading is that a citation for B041 can be written, so your condition may well be met, but a good citation does not change the fact that the prize would honour a measurement technology. I would also note, with thanks, your disclosure on B020 and your decision to keep it only as an alternative; I agree with that handling and it removes the need for further discussion of B020 from my side.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B018 first but doubts the claim that Kane and Mele's prediction was promptly realised, and asks whether the decisive discovery in B041 is the lattice scheme or the later metrological performance.
responses.response: On B018 we agree. The experiment followed the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, so I would not describe the realisation as a direct test of Kane and Mele alone. What links the credited names is that Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 classification and the general helical-edge argument, and the HgTe experiment tested that physics. I think the deliberation should say so explicitly, and this is better than claiming a clean chain. On your B041 question, my view is that the credited discovery would have to be the magic-wavelength lattice, with the performance at 1e-18 as demonstration, otherwise the citation drifts into engineering progress and loses its distinction from 2005 and 2012.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to B018 after ranking DMFT (B009) first, and argues that Kane and Mele's Z2 invariant and graphene proposal are logically independent of the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal.
responses.response: I find your independence argument persuasive on the theory side: the Z2 invariant and the general argument for helical edge states do not depend on HgTe, and that is why Kane and Mele are credited for the prediction. It does not remove the experimental-side problem, however. Molenkamp chose HgTe because of the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang calculation, and the credited trio does not include the people who made the material-specific proposal. I would keep the two points separate in the citation language: the theory credit is for the symmetry-based prediction, and the experimental credit is for the observation of edge transport in HgTe wells. That is the most honest way to describe what the three names did.

uncertainties: Whether the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, with Zhang deceased, is acceptable to the committee even with a narrow citation, or whether it makes the three-name set unfair.
Whether the committee reads the Z2 time-reversal-invariant class as distinct from the 2016 prize, as I do, or as overlapping.
Whether the 3D topological-insulator discoveries can be kept outside a citation bounded by the quantum spin Hall effect without a priority dispute.
Whether a measurement technology and its performance (B041) should weigh equally with a new phase of matter; this is a judgment about the will, not something the file settles.
I rely on recollection of the priority history and have not verified it independently.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B018 or the alternatives B041 and B030. My documented connections (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur, KTH) do not include any named candidate. My astroparticle background had earlier inclined me towards B016 (IceCube), which I no longer list; this is an updated disclosure from round 1, in which I listed B016 as an alternative.
